It models the conditional probability of one class as a function of the predictors. For a binary response, write $$ Y\in\{0,1\}. $$ The goal is to estimate $$ \Prob(Y=1\mid X=x). $$ This probability can then be used for two tasks: - probability estimation, - classification by thresholding the probability. ## Modeling Binary Outcomes In linear regression, we model a quantitative response by $$ Y=\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\cdots+\beta_px_p+\epsilon. $$ This is not appropriate for a binary response. A linear model can produce fitted values below 0 or above 1, so its fitted values cannot always be interpreted as probabilities. Logistic regression instead models $$ \pi(x) = \Prob(Y=1\mid X=x) $$ using the logistic function: $$ \pi(x) = \frac{ \exp(\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\cdots+\beta_px_p) }{ 1+\exp(\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\cdots+\beta_px_p) }. $$ Let $$ \eta(x)=\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\cdots+\beta_px_p. $$ Then $$ \pi(x)=\frac{e^{\eta(x)}}{1+e^{\eta(x)}}. $$ This always lies between 0 and 1. ::: {.callout-note} ## Main idea Logistic regression is linear in the log-odds, not in the probability. ::: ## Odds and the Logit Link The odds of class 1 are $$ \frac{\pi(x)}{1-\pi(x)}. $$ For logistic regression, $$ 1-\pi(x) = \frac{1}{1+e^{\eta(x)}}. $$ Therefore $$ \frac{\pi(x)}{1-\pi(x)} = e^{\eta(x)}. $$ Taking logs gives $$ \log\left( \frac{\pi(x)}{1-\pi(x)} \right) = \eta(x) = \beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\cdots+\beta_px_p. $$ The function $$ \log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right) $$ is called the logit function. Logistic regression is a generalized linear model with a Bernoulli response and logit link. ## Interpreting Coefficients The coefficients are interpreted through odds ratios. Suppose all predictors except $x_j$ are fixed. If $x_j$ increases by one unit, then the log-odds increase by $$ \beta_j. $$ Exponentiating gives $$ \text{odds ratio}=e^{\beta_j}. $$ Thus: - $\beta_j$ is the change in log-odds for a one-unit increase in $x_j$; - $e^{\beta_j}$ is the multiplicative change in the odds. ::: {.callout-caution} ## Not a probability change A logistic regression coefficient is not a direct change in probability. The probability change depends on the current value of all predictors. ::: For example, if $\beta_j=0.05$, then $$ e^{0.05}\approx 1.051. $$ Holding other predictors fixed, a one-unit increase in $x_j$ multiplies the odds by about $1.051$, or increases the odds by about $5.1\%$. ## From Probability to Classification After fitting the model, the estimated probability is $$ \hat\pi(x)=\widehat{\Prob}(Y=1\mid X=x). $$ A common classification rule is $$ \hat Y = \begin{cases} 1, & \hat\pi(x)>0.5,\\ 0, & \hat\pi(x)\le 0.5. \end{cases} $$ The threshold does not have to be 0.5. If false positives and false negatives have different costs, the threshold should reflect those costs. ## A One-Variable Calculation Suppose the fitted model is $$ \log\left(\frac{\pi(x)}{1-\pi(x)}\right) = -3.006+0.052x. $$ For a subject with $x=55$, $$ \eta(55) = -3.006+0.052(55) = -0.146. $$ The estimated probability is $$ \pi(55) = \frac{e^{-0.146}}{1+e^{-0.146}} \approx 0.463. $$ So the model estimates a class-1 probability of about $46.3\%$. ## Estimation by Maximum Likelihood For observation $i$, let $$ \pi_i=\pi(x_i). $$ Since $Y_i$ is binary, $$ Y_i\mid X_i=x_i \sim \operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_i). $$ The probability mass function is $$ \Prob(Y_i=y_i\mid X_i=x_i) = \pi_i^{y_i}(1-\pi_i)^{1-y_i}. $$ For independent observations, the likelihood is $$ L(\beta) = \prod_{i=1}^n \pi_i^{y_i}(1-\pi_i)^{1-y_i}. $$ The log-likelihood is $$ \ell(\beta) = \sum_{i=1}^n \left[ y_i\log(\pi_i) + (1-y_i)\log(1-\pi_i) \right]. $$ Using the logistic form, this can be written as $$ \ell(\beta) = \sum_{i=1}^n \left[ y_i x_i^\top\beta - \log\{1+\exp(x_i^\top\beta)\} \right]. $$ Logistic regression does not have the same closed-form solution as ordinary least squares. The coefficients are found by numerical optimization, commonly Newton-type methods. ## Deviance In logistic regression and other generalized linear models, deviance measures lack of fit. Two common quantities are: - null deviance: deviance for an intercept-only model; - residual deviance: deviance for the fitted model. A large reduction from null deviance to residual deviance means the predictors explain useful information about the class probabilities. ## Logistic Regression in `statsmodels` `statsmodels` is useful when the goal is classical statistical output: coefficient tables, standard errors, z-statistics, and p-values. Common metrics include: - accuracy, - sensitivity or recall, - specificity, - precision, - F1 score, - ROC AUC, - log loss. ::: {#34f06e4e .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} from sklearn.metrics import classification_report, roc_auc_score, log_loss pipe = Pipeline( steps=[ ("scaler", StandardScaler()), ("model", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)), ] ) pipe.fit(X_train, y_train) pred = pipe.predict(X_test) prob = pipe.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1] print(classification_report(y_test, pred)) print("ROC AUC:", roc_auc_score(y_test, prob)) print("Log loss:", log_loss(y_test, prob)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` precision recall f1-score support 0 0.89 0.75 0.81 64 1 0.86 0.94 0.90 107 accuracy 0.87 171 macro avg 0.88 0.85 0.86 171 weighted avg 0.87 0.87 0.87 171 ROC AUC: 0.9452394859813085 Log loss: 0.27607434046241025 ``` ::: ::: Probability-based metrics such as log loss evaluate the quality of the predicted probabilities, not only the final class labels. ## Summary Logistic regression: - models binary outcomes through class probabilities; - uses the logit link to make log-odds linear in the predictors; - estimates coefficients by maximum likelihood; - interprets coefficients through odds ratios; - produces both probabilities and class predictions; - has a linear decision boundary in the original predictors; - is often combined with regularization in predictive workflows.
